name: Monkey Skin
lede: Monkey Skin is a light reddish brown dated by Maerz and Paul to 1927, and our graph's nearest named neighbor for it, Reddish Grey, differs mainly by being a touch redder.

sections.title: A 1927 trade name, undocumented further
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates Monkey Skin to 1927, plate 5, row B, column 9, and separately records a close neighbor on the same plate, Rose Blush, from a year earlier [1]. Why the animal was chosen as the reference, rather than any of the many other brown-naming conventions in the same dictionary, is undocumented in the sources we hold [1][4]. No book held in color-kb discusses this name [4].

Its nearest distinct named neighbor is [[reddish-grey]], 2.7 units off and "redder" by our graph's own description, with [[rose-brown]] and [[vinaceous-brown]] close by at 4.0 [3]. A fourth cousin in the library, slightly cooler and greyer, is [[taupe]] [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds Monkey Skin in 360 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.5 percent, as photographed [2]. Its rate is unusually high in a narrow fifteenth-century window, the 1420s, 8.6 times the archive's overall rate, alongside a broader twentieth-century rise [2]. Counts are computed matches on varnished, photographed paintings, not pigment identifications [2]. Its company in the 1420s window is mostly devotional and portrait painting, not a single workshop or region we can name from the data alone [2].
